concepts.def: Two-class model: bourgeoisie own means of production, proletariat sell labour; objective class position drives conflict.
Class (market position), status (prestige) and party (power) are three dimensions of stratification.
1980 Nuffield study: seven-class scheme based on employment relations; basis of NS-SEC used by ONS.
Neo-Marxist: contradictory class locations (managers) hold authority but sell labour; expands Marx's binary.
Davis and Moore (1945): inequality is necessary to motivate the most talented to fill the most important positions.
Murray (1990): welfare-dependent group with deviant values; criticised for blaming victims of structural disadvantage.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Researching & Understanding Social Inequalities — a core area of A-Level Sociology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Researching & Understanding Social Inequalities brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Researching & Understanding Social Inequalities.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Why do sociologists use official statistics on inequality cautiously?
options: Their level of education only.
Statistics cannot measure inequality at all.
Official statistics are always perfectly objective.
Because they can be socially constructed and may hide or distort real differences.

mcqs.q: Is social class the only form of inequality sociologists study?
options: No - they also study gender, ethnicity, age and disability.
Only class inequality matters.
Inequality no longer exists in modern society.
Statistics cannot measure inequality at all.

mcqs.q: What does the Goldthorpe scheme classify people by?
options: Statistics cannot measure inequality at all.
Their income alone.
Their occupation and employment relations (their market and work situation).
Their level of education only.

sequence.def: Inequality research starts with a precise question
Class, gender or ethnicity become measurable indicators
Questions are written to capture the indicators
A small trial finds confusing or leading items
Main data collection across the chosen sample
Patterns of inequality are drawn from the data
